name: New Brunswick
summary_text: Visitors in New Brunswick stand under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.  Provincial education policy is the layer where New Brunswick differs from the rest of Canada. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development took effect on 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them informally in school, with parental consent encouraged but not required; formal use of a chosen name in official records for a student under 16 still requires parental consent. The revision was made by the Holt government and goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.  The application clause of Policy 713 covers the school environment as a whole and names the people it binds: all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A non-resident present in a New Brunswick classroom, whether as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer, is therefore subject to the same name, pronoun and privacy rules as a pupil.  The 2023 revisions remain the reference point for what the province is capable of imposing. Changes taking effect on 1 July 2023 barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in accordance with their gender identity. The Progressive Conservative government of Premier Blaine Higgs made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed, eight party members including six cabinet ministers boycotted question period over the handling of the file, and dissidents called for a leadership review. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests outside the legislature and a constitutional challenge by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.  Facilities are addressed by Policy 713 as originally written: the 2020 policy requires schools to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Whether that requirement survives verbatim in the text revised on 1 January 2025 is not established by the sources.  In federal custody, the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents. Requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists under the service's 2022 gender-diversity policy. As of 2025 the service recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's; between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 requests from people assigned male at birth for placement in women's institutions, with 35 approved, 72 denied and 22 withdrawn. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the unclear health-or-safety override and the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. This federal policy is the framework a trans person in federal custody in New Brunswick stands under.

name: Newfoundland and Labrador
summary_text: Newfoundland and Labrador stands under the Canadian federal framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial healthcare coverage is universal.  Legal gender recognition in the province operates without a surgery requirement. An amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009, given Royal Assent 13 April 2016, removed the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with a December 2015 ruling of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission on complaints brought by two trans women.  A second amendment, given Royal Assent 23 June 2021, extended the route to residents who were not born in the province but have lived there at least three months. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and can be used to update records in other jurisdictions; it serves as the identification document for people born outside Canada. The same amendment aligned with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.  Current requirements on the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador's official page: applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s, with consent of the other parent or guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months. There is no fee for the change application itself; charges apply only to official copies of updated documents ($35 for a new birth certificate, $30 online).  One documented cross-border caveat applies. The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate carrying an X gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations, so a provincial record with that marker may not travel cleanly.  Police-reported hate-crime data is favourable for the province but rests on small numbers. Statistics Canada (30 March 2026 release, 2024 data) recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% jump the previous year, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, tied with Manitoba, against Ontario's highest at 16.0. The province's recorded rise of 51% reflects 19 incidents in 2023 against 29 in 2024, so the percentage change is statistically fragile. Police figures capture only reported incidents. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report examines national police-reported data including offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; Egale Canada is an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

sources.title: Egan v. Canada, [1995] - Supreme Court of Canada
sources.documents: Landmark ruling that sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under s.15 equality clause of the Canadian Charter as an analogous ground - provides constitutional equality framework enforceable in Newfoundland and Labrador.
sources.detail: Citation detail visible: 'In a landmark decision in 1995, Egan v Canada, the Supreme Court of Canada held that sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause' and 'declared that sexual orientation was included within the bounds of section 15, as an analogous ground.' sources.title: Vriend v Alberta, [1998] - Supreme Court of Canada
sources.documents: Held failure of provincial legislature to include sexual orientation as prohibited ground in human rights law was itself a violation of s.15 Charter rights - led to requirement that all provinces/territories including Newfoundland and Labrador cover sexual orientation and later gender identity.
sources.detail: Citation detail visible: 'In its 1998 decision in Vriend v Alberta, the Supreme Court found the failure of the provincial legislature to include sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination in its human rights law was itself a violation of section 15 Charter rights.' No URL visible.
